text:
You Rule, Not Nvidia or EVGA or even LTT (though LTT is awesome!), but you Anthony need give no apologies for telling us the unbiased Truth! 

That Calm and focused drive to the core Truth of the products and topics you explore is the reason Folks like I watch and, in my 48 hour no sleep odd minded state, thought "we  should all be Printing small golden Anthony Buddhas that have a button that alternates phrases like "Research First" and "Hype is Not Performance!"

No Im not a crazy Stalker, I am suffering from insomnia a need to overshare but yourvid made me slow down and think and appreciate there are good reviews out there and I don't have to be a constant victim to Advertising and Hype... 
My Story:
I have not watched many tech videos recently, In fact I cant remember the last time I turned on Youtube for more than 15 minutes and then only to check on the latest news from the FED and how it would affect Crypto (I know you already hate me) So When I did watch a Click Bait Video Entitled EVGA STOPS MAKING GPUs... I Panicked...
 "OMG EVGA is Stopping GPU Production! I'm an EVGA Fanboy 4 Life (we will see, but ASUS is already banned from my builds) and my most recent CARD is the OG 1080 FTW Card and I had planned to Upgrade to a 5000 or better when I could to Finish My EVGA Z390 all EVGA Build (Mainly for work and VR)! ...but Now The EVGA 3000 cards that were "Discounted" are at a premium and getting more expensive as they sell out and THERE WILL NEVER BE MORE! 
I0 need One NOW! 2 Hours Later found and ordered near New EVGA 3090 Ti FTW3 with Warranty using Make an Offer on eBay for 1200 with S/H... acceptable.... 

NOT ACCEPTABLE? = Did NO Research! Didn't Know about 4000 Series! (Life has been busy, I used to watch LTT daily) I have Shamed The Tech Nerd Name! 

This Is why we need your calm but poignant truth to help those of us who sometimes go astray because we once fell hard for a smaller more effective manufacturer when their cards were barely a 30 dollar difference, if that... 

Now, how am I going to pay back the money I borrowed, get a stronger PSU and upgrade from that i5 my friend donated to my build to actually make this 3090t Ti even worth while? Time will tell, But I got The Last Best EVGA card EVER! Right? …. right...? 

Pray for my Fanboy Soul oh Wise One... 

PS - I'm not crazy or a stalker just been trying to earn money trading crypto for about 40 hours straight and took a break to watch some LTT about my new card and thought Id show my appreciation for insights learned with a bit of creative writing and humor : ) 


Cheers! 

-Ed

text: It's actually good that people are willing to buy beastly cards. They are helping to fund the transition to 4K high refresh. As people get these cards, it becomes profitable for monitor manufacturers to build 4K high refresh panels. The more beastly cards, the more the demand for better monitors. The more demand, the better the economies of scale for the manufacturer (GPU and monitor makers alike). Ten years ago, OLED TVs were $15,000 US. Now, you can find 4K 120hz OLED TVs for $900. I'm more than happy some people paid the extreme premium for the new tech so that LG etc. could make more OLEDs at lower price points.

text: I think that a large part of what drives the demand for these GPUs is VR.  Even this 3090 Ti wouldn't have enough horsepower to run a flight simulator in 100% resolution with anti-aliasing (let alone supersampling), and get true 90 FPS without reprojection.  For a few years there we were at a spot where the GPU hardware was ahead of, or at least on par with, the display hardware.  But the insane pixel count of VR has flipped that equation around.  Hopefully we will see software advances in eye-tracking and foveated rendering to reduce the ever-increasing demands of VR headsets.

text: I think it is at that price not to sell 3090tis but to boost the sales of 3090s at current prices.  People already have in their minds what they believe is the value of whatever item they want to buy before they even walk into a store.  By having a similar item that is marginally better but at a significantly higher pricing you are playing with people's perceived value of the lesser item.  The 3090 is generally perceived as prohibitively expensive but by having the ridiculously overpriced 3090ti on the shelf next to it the 3090 now appears to be of better value even though the price hasn't change.  You see this tactic often in stores.  You'll have a $300 pair of shoes right next to a $150 pair of shoes so that people will buy the $150 shoes instead of the $120 pair they would have bought if the $300 pair wasn't there.

text:
mmm, as a 3090 owner, Id like to point out a reason as to why at least there are quite a few 3090 owners despite the price, and seemingly no good reason to buy one for gaming.

GPU raytrace rendering for vfx, realtime Product design reviews,  Cinematics.
Its faster than Cpu rendering and takes the job that was once in the realm of render farms.
However it burns through a huge amount of Vram for even small environments when Raytacing is doing its thing.
and when they hit max the vram, render jobs just tend to just crash letting users wake up in the morning to night of no renders done.

this is true across the board in Vray, Blender, arnold, and particularly Unreal raytracing for cinematics, 11 or 12 gigs of vram just dont cut it if you wanna render 4K engineering products in open environments.

if it wernt for the 3090's Id be seriously looking at A6000  which is priced at "wtf" level.

I know this is seperate to the fact that the 3090ti is really useless, even for me with the same vram.

but i wanted to address the existing market that likes the 3090's

I think this channel doesnt often look at that angle of the market(though it may be niche) and assumes its just nvidia fanboys or power hungry gamers... (and yeah if AMD had a gpu that actually had good raytracing performance, with large vram, Id look at it too.. but nope.)

text:
I think you'll find it has ECC support because GDDR6X's PAM4 signaling  REQUIRES extensive error correction just to function.
PAM4 cant physically slew from a "00" state to a "11" state  or "11" to "00" in a single clock (at the speeds it is used).  so any time 1100 or 0011 appears it has to say something completely different and rely on ECC to detect checkbits and correct it. - This is a bit stupid and shows that Nvidia are only using 6X for marketing as the "G6X can transmit twice as much data in the same period of time as GDDR6X" that Jensen claimed at the ampere Keynote was total BS.  - not only is does 6X NEED to be clocked much slower to even function; it also requires large amounts of additional checkbits in the data stream. 
Their memory bandwidth can still be advertised as super high on paper, but 1/4 of that bandwidth is consumed just by the ecc data. and with the lower clocks; that "x2" becomes about "x1.2" ACTUAL useful boost.

text:
@AndyOO6  man, no.
Yes, it’s possible to reach 1000W, the problem is that the rise in wattage is directly proportional to the temperature, if it reached a 1000W, the TDP would be 1000W, and it isn’t that easy to cool a thing like that. 
A 5000W power supply is almost impossible to happen because of cooling, stability and size.
And don’t forget that GPUs need to go into laptops too.
It’s almost irrealistic to say that it’ll reach 1000w, although it’s possible, it’s really hard to reach it, and the card would need more time to release, since nVidia would need to wait for new power supplies that can actually carry it (since a 1000W GPU would be used with a CPU like the I9, R9 or Threadripper Pro.

text: Watts do matter.  It;s a fools buy. Basically, a card like this is a space heater that gives slightly prettier pictures than other ones and cost you more to operate than heating your house.  If you live in Alaska - it may make sense. Open your breaker box.  A typical US circuit for a room with 3 outlets and a room light has them all on a 15-20 amp breaker.  That is 1500 to  2400 watts AC for the entire room.  With an 80+ PSU - depending on your house's setup - that is 1200-1900 watts max for everything on that circuit including the room lights and anything plugged in.  If your card is pulling 1200 watts alone, you have between 0 (yea....none) and 700 watts (most likely ~500) to power everything else on the circuit.  Including your computer and all the cooling you will require to keep things cooled down - because frankly - this is a brut-force card probably running at <50% efficiency watt for watt and providing almost imperceptible improvements.  And then, after raising your electricity bill through the roof - they have the audacity to ask for >2K.  Lol - Nice.  This is an insult to me - an Nvidia fan.....or I was.  And I don't like AMD........I am going out back to rub stick together.

text: I don't really mind the power draw, since your charts do show its basically proportional to performance. There are professional applications (not many, but some) where a couple percent performance uplift at a couple percent higher power usage could just barely make sense, provided high enough utilization to overcome the purchase price but low enough to not force just buying more smaller cards. But that purchase price is so dumb, and squeezes out even more of that already thin window of viability. I accept that there is generally sublinear performance gains vs cost, but this is way too far, even 3090 was pushing it. If these are just higher-binned 3090s that happened to come out better in the randomness of semiconductor manufacturing, thats cool and by all means sell them, but they should be priced accordingly. I suspect Nvidia may have put themselves in a position where they felt they had to charge more for this card to recoup the expenses of developing a higher performance cooler and power delivery for a product that they wouldn't be able to sell many of anyway, but there's gotta be a way to increase commonality with lower end cards to address that. Or just skip the air cooler entirely, I can't imagine many users of this thing wanting air cooling on a card of this magnitude anyway

text:
Node shrinks have not been delivering improved power efficiency per transistor like they used to have been. This is an uncomfortable fact that you're going to have to deal with and either you'll have to accept performance increases stalling out as we can't continue to scale transistor counts, or you'll have to accept needing to push more power to get faster performance.

It's OK to admit that we can't really get much more performance out considering how nice many games already look, but if you really want RT lighting and reflections in gaming fact is you'll need more performance than we currently have.

Also, 500W is pretty insane and cooling that beast is gonna be wild, people are no doubt going to be talking about how bad this is for the environment. Lets put it in perspective here: I live in San Diego. Electricity is around 36 cents/kWh here and looking at my local utility's sustainability statement, it appears that each kWh generated is an average of 243 g CO2 emitted. If I've got one of these guys AND a 12900k running full tilt (250W, but in reality gaming rarely if ever comes close to that, but lets overestimate anyway), my computer will be running close to 850W. If I spend 6 hours straight gaming, I've spent about $1.80 in electricity for the day, and emitted 1.25 kG CO2. Now, say I want to instead go over to the beach, about a 5 mile drive away from me, and I own the most efficient EV, a Model 3 (0.24 kWh/mile). In that 10 mile round trip drive doing something environmentally friendly and outdoorsy, I've used 2.4 kWh of electricity versus the 2.2 kWh gaming that entire 6 hours. Now which hobby is more destructive to the environment?

You guys seem out of touch with the actual buyers who NEED a GPU like this and it seems clear you don't have anyone like that on staff. Anthony also seems really condescending here as a result to people like me who really need a GPU that is better than the 3090.
I NEED a GPU like the 3090ti, I actually need a better GPU than the 3090ti. If you guys were VR sim racers and actually knew how to setup a Pimax 8K+/8KX for clarity you might understand the niche group of people who actually really need GPU's better than a 3090 and your own benchmarks here show that the 3090ti would be a significant upgrade for someone like me. You see for me the only benchmark that is relevant is the minimum frames at 4k because I'm actually pushing more than 4k pixels and in VR sim racing the only fps that matters is minimum because you can't have any dips in FPS and you must set your refresh rate in your Pimax based on your minimum fps for consistency. So based on your benchmarks a 3090ti will allow me to choose between running 90hz over my current 75hz with my 3090 or I could run at 140hFOV instead of my current 120hFOV. 
The reason I'll probably not buy the 3090ti is the price and timing because the Pimax 12k is coming before the end of the year and because of superior eye tracking and foveated rendering might be easier to run than the current Pimax and the next gen GPU's might be available at the same time. I don't know how much I'll be out of pocket if I sell my 3090 and buy a 3090ti when they become available here but I can imagine based on the 33% retail price increase over the 3090 so if that means I'll be out of pocket approximately 1k AUD for a few months of extra enjoyment, that's just too much for me and I'll possibly just choose to suffer with my 3090 for now.

If anyone at LTT actually reads this. If you want to get the best clarity out of your Pimax possible, you must run render quality in Pitool at 1.5  with 100% steam VR custom render resolution in a Pimax 8K+ which is the same as running an 8KX in upscale mode. I don't have a 8KX to test and it might be that at native resolution a higher render quality is less noticeable but considering it has been well documented on forums that a render quality of 1 makes visual sacrifices I suspect that 1.5 or at least 1.25 would still be necessary for optimal clarity in the 8KX. text: Can you guys please do a comprehensive breakdown of performance per watt from the 900 series onwards? I feel like the architectural changes we've been experiencing over the last 5-10 years or so aren't really as large as they appear, especially for those on a limited power budget. Sure, a 100W bump in power is negligible in terms of how much it'll cost extra per month to pay for that electricity (maybe $1-2 at the worst), but the real kicker is if you need to buy a new PSU, new cables, new case...then things start getting a bit hairy. But if you're a datacenter, or an engineering firm running CAD/CFD/simulations all day, every day, or a video editing house, and you have maybe a hundred or two hundred of these things, now you're looking at an extra thousand or two per month. Again, doesn't sound like much in the context of a small-to-medium-sized business. But if your previous GPUs drew 350W on average, and your new ones draw 450W, and you spent a quarter million on them ALREADY...ehhhh.

author: @T3ddyRuxp1n

text: ​ @T3ddyRuxp1n  2000w is not possible, the upper limits of possibility is 800w (with air cooling) after that it has to be water (which wont get to 2000w unless somesort of in die cooling is used) then it will be exotic. The problem is we cant just keep shrinking nodes like we used to in the next decade we will likely hit the physical boundary of whats possible. Once this happens we will likely see another clockspeed war (where companies go and try to make clock speeds as high as possible 10+ghz) but that also has it's limits, Once that happens developers will be forced to learn how to multithread better on games. That again has it's limits, this will likely force new architectures and new ways of processing things x86 will die something will take it's place. While this happens we will get rid of silicon and use a better material such as diamond (which has 22 times the heat transfer of silicon and can handle 5 times the heat without degrading (we will likely see chips running at 400c) this will further allow us to add more wattage to it. After this I simply dont know where we could go, we will likely discover new ways to compute stuff however if we dont it could be the end of increasing computing power without increasing size. (there is a theoretical end point to where its impossible to get more computing power out of something even if you add more power)

So to add to this, a standard North american home electrical circuit will be on a 15 amp breaker.  15 amps x 120 VAC = 1800 Watts.  At the point where our PCs start drawing 1500 watts we will probably need to start changing the wiring in our homes.  And how far away from 1500watts are we?  I'm guessing 2 years or less, Ryzen 7 is supposed to have a huge performance boost over Ryzen 5, and even the AMD 7xxx series is being reported to have huge performance gains over previous gen.

Might need to wire a 30 amp circuit so you can run your PC and an air conditioner at the same time,  a 3090ti would probably heat a well insulated house.
author: @T3ddyRuxp1n

text:
@T3ddyRuxp1n  I don't know all the specifics, but in the USA, all new homes have to have way more electrical infrastructure than previously. There was a recent code update which mandates, among other things, dedicated 20a circuits in the garage (for EV charging), and way more power going to the kitchen. I think most new homes are also wired with 20a circuits.
But yeah, those with older houses really should look into upgrading their electrical wiring if they want to use these new components. Especially considering that old wiring and breakers could have degraded and may not support full power safely anymore.
author: @macattack123mattc3

text: @T3ddyRuxp1n  Excellent point. We live in a society where everyone is trying to be energy efficient and environmentally responsible then we have video cards going the opposite way.
author: @phishstikV

text: @macattack123mattc3  Most kitchens do several 20A circuits for countertop microwaves and toasters, etc, which requires 12 gauge wire, but most bedrooms only have 15A circuits with the thinner 14 gauge wire. Either way the individual outlets can only handle 15A, and you have some overhead for things like a UPS, so yeah it is pretty conceivable that you are looking at some pretty hot wires as you approach those limits for extended periods. Heaters are restricted to 1500 watts (rather than the full 1800) because they consider it unsafe to design a continuous load at the max.

text:
I really don't like the direction Nvidia is going in with their new GPUs requiring insane amounts of power. Energy isn't getting any cheaper and nobody enjoys being strong-armed into upgrading their PSU. I have a really nice 850W PSU, I'm not spending $200 to upgrade it just so I can power an inefficient brute-force 4000 series GPU. 

As usual, big businesses are letting investors and whales influence their decisions at the expense of everyone else. Even though the 3090 only represents 0.5% of the user base, it's probably closer to 1-2% dollar for dollar since it costs 2-4x more than every other card. Nvidia is selling A LOT of these cards. I'm sure the extreme scarcity of the 3080 hasn't helped, but it seems like the demographic of people who must have the absolute best no matter the cost is bigger than previously thought. 

Nvidia's marketing is absolutely shameful too. 8K gaming isn't real. 8K monitors barely exist. Most 8K TVs cost more than a PC with a 3090Ti in it. 4K gaming is not obsolete, in fact the 3000 series made it much more accessible than ever before. Despite this, 4K gaming is still out of reach for most people so I have no idea why anyone would think 8K is feasible in the slightest.

text:
This is where I return to my argument that we are pushing games too far in the wrong direction. 

I believe games have been beautiful for years. Almost too beautiful, too distracting. Shooters with visual data soup and beautification that detracts from the loop. RPG’s trying their utmost to reflect reality to a still pixelated N’th degree. Etc. 

This odd westward expansion style of gaming has been destroying the consumer market, clearly shown in full focus what happens when we focus on the next best thing and the heights of performance without care for efficiency, affordability, or compatibility. 

It is another unsustainable system in a tangled skein of other unsustainable systems, except now the fan-blown waste is hitting our games.

To change it we as gamers, as with any unsustainable system, must consistently agree that this is not something we condone.

That said, this 3090ti looks like really expensive E-waste after it fries my 1950’s wiring in my old home. Anthony did a great job here, I love the stance.

text:
I spent nearly a year trying to get lucky when GPUs dropped trying to get a 3080. I wanted to replace my 2080 with something newer because I'm plugging into a TV with HDMI instead of a monitor with DP nowadays. I did end up getting lucky in finally being able to actually cart and purchase a new GPU, it just.. wasn't the 3080 I wanted, but a 3080 ti. Spending nearly double what I had initially wanted was a bit of a drag, especially since I ended up needing a new PSU on top of that (and high powered SFX units aren't cheap).

I think this thing is close enough to the 3090 to say I have close to what peak performance is, and it's plugged into a 4k 120hz TV to get the most out of it. And I can say now, it's not really worth the difference. The money I spent on the TV, or the speakers I got to complete the setup were a much better use of money. The thing with cards at the top is that they're in a kind of annoying place to be. You want the absolute best of the best, that's why you get them, but the reality is I still can't just tick everything to 4k Ultra and have it push out all the frames I want. In the games I can, I basically could in my 2080 as well. And in the ones that I really went from a generally poor experience to a good one, like CP2077 with RT on, I would have gotten just about as good as I have now with a 3080 or even 3070. 

Most of the games I play end up being in one of those two situations, where I either already had more than enough performance on an old card, or am still unable to get things turned up to 11 at full res and FPS. There's very few situations a 3090 or ti is going to be enough of a difference over a reasonable card to actually matter. As with all halo products, price-to-performance ratio left the conversation a while before we got to this thing. If you have enough money that an extra $500-1000 for a GPU just doesn't matter, you do you. Go for it, get the best of the best. But for anyone else, if buying it is within the total you can spend, but that money isn't insignificant, I think you'd get a lot more out of getting a more reasonable card like a 3080 and using that money to upgrade some other part, or buy more games, or save it for a next gen card or something.

text:
I built a nice PC like 5 years ago for under $2000 CAD (that actually accounts for minor upgrades since then, including swapping out a GTX 1070 for a used 1080 ti).  While it is showing its age a bit in the CPU department (i5 6600k OC'd to 4.5ghz) and isn't anywhere close to as powerful as current higher end PC's, it still works great at 1440p/144hz, often hitting 80fps+ on max settings in many fairly graphically intensive games.  The point is, it's a 5 year old PC that cost far less than a single 3090 ti (MSRP is over $2500 CAD) and it is perfectly fine for gaming purposes in 2022 for an average gamer that isn't chasing 4k, ray tracing, or insane fps.  1440p/144hz is the sweet spot for gaming still, almost no PC gamers have a better monitor than this, or they are using a 4k 60hz TV which is more of a console gaming thing.  

People really need to calm down with the PC overkill.  I get that there will always be enthusiasts out there, or people with a lot of money and super high end TVs and monitors.  That's who these cards are for.  But that should be less than 1% of gamers.  Most gamers can get fantastic performance, well enough for their needs, with a 3060 or 3070.  That's the mainstream consumer high end at this point.  Even a 3080 is overkill for the vast majority of people.  This whole insane chip shortage and scalping issue never would have had anywhere close to the level of impact it had if average gamers were more reasonable and simply refused to spend over $500-600 on a card.  I'm not trying to tell people what to buy, but it just makes no sense to pay double or triple the price for a completely unnecessary 3080 or 3090 just so you can say you hit some bench test score.  Please people, stop the madness.  

And yes, I'm aware that I'm using a top tier card from 2 generations ago, but I bought it used out of a mining rig and even retail 1080 ti's were fairly reasonably priced back then compared to now.

text:
@artemaung5274  The "60" series is always a double edged sword in each generation. On release they are amazing value, very little compromised compared to their "bigger brothers" and can burn through every new release but doesn't age as well as the 70 and 80 series and is significantly less "future proof". 

The 980 is still a capable card at 1080p today and the 970 is clinging on for most games if you can live with very low settings. The 960 stopped being viable years ago. 

You are now starting to the see the same thing with the 10 series - with 1080s going strong and 1070s starting to struggle and 1060s becoming less and less capable of running new releases. 

I suspect soon its the turn of the 2060 - we are already seeing it dropping down to "minimum specs" for many new releases. 

My view is that if you want to stick with the card as long as possible and want best value for money in the long term invest in a "80" series. But if you want the best value for money within the shorter term, within the current generation and don't mind having to upgrade a bit earlier, then "60" series are the best value for money. The "70" is a bit of "goldilocks" in that it lasts longer than the 60 but you will end up compromising a lot more on settings quality than the 80 series in later life.

text:
@JimIBobIJones  

Okay I got an easier explanation, that's hopefully you can understand:

When you sort GPU's by it's price/performance you notice it tends to always be worse and worse the higher you go. 

But (important note!) this curve isn't always smooth.

Few examples: 1050 was best in price/performance among 10-series GPUs, but 1060 3Gb was almost identical in price/performance while 1050 Ti was worse in price/performance vs both. So among those 3 1060 3Gb was a very clear winner in terms of total performance and price/performance.

Similar story with 1060 3Gb, 1060 6Gb and 1070.  1060 3Gb and 1070 are staying closer to better part of the curve while 1060 6Gb is a worse outlier. If you wanted a card that's faster than 1060 3Gb, best deal was 1070 - not 1060 6Gb.

Again similar story with 1070, 1080 and 1080 Ti. 1080 was a worse outlier on this curve, but 1070 and 1080 Ti were on a better part of the curve.

1650 was very poor value GPU that was worse than both 1060 3Gb and 1060 6Gb. I didn't make any sense at all. But it's successor 1650 Super was amazing beating anything ever in price/performance even up to today in 2022.

20super gen had the smoothest curve of all. There weren't any clear outliers like in 20-series or in 10-series. 2070 Super was maybe best deal in the lineup, but the difference is a lot more subtle.

30-series are very bad in low end, but amazing in high end which is to say 30-series curve got a lot more "flatter". 3080 basically has been a king in value from this "curve" perspective. 

So your point "80 always gives better longevity" varies quite significantly depending on generation/iteration.

also xx80 represents very different price brackets. 

So my point is getting the best curve outlier (better deal) is the better strategy and you can combine it regardless where you are on price/bracket.

You want to go for high end? Sure it makes sense. But again I wouldn't go with 1080 in 2016. It was a bad deal. 1080 degraded from high end to mid-range in 3 years. 
2060 is still midrange after 3 years and still able to play games at 100+fps in 1440p.

So even though more expensive card in principle should always last longer than cheaper card, sometimes there are outliers like those which makes 2060 longer lasting than 1080.

So yeah, maybe this isn't not quite aligning to my original simple comment, but hopefully this clears misunderstanding.

text:
The implications of your PC running 16-18 hours a day notwithstanding, it sounds like your rig could do with some top-to-bottom efficiency optimization. The potential for savings generally is substantial.

BIOS level -
Look for Energy Star or CEC options to turn on, as well as ErP.
Failing that, turn on ASPM for PCIe (it rarely is by default). (Note - you may need to customize your Windows power plan and set PCIe power savings to maximum.)
Make sure C-states for the processor are enabled (note: package C6 and up can be problematic on Ryzen, though I don't think you can even go past C3 with a GPU installed).
Make sure STA LPM is enabled.
Turn off XMP, which may interfere with the memory controller's ability to clock down in idle. If that leaves you at 2133 since that's all the SPD has to offer, well, sucks to be you. No, just kidding, if you can't dial in e.g. 2666 at 19-19-19-44-63 or 2400 at 17-17-17-40-57 manually with DIMMs at 1.20 V without issues, you can always get a plain vanilla 3000 (CL21) or 3200 (CL22) kit sans XMP and flog your old RAM on eBay. I wouldn't hope for more than the 2700's official maximum of 2933 in any case.
There have been cases where a BIOS update alone has improved idle power consumption. A good opportunity to check for whether Ryzen 5000 support has been added. If not, I would price out a B550 - 5700G (or 5800) combo. 50% more oomph is nothing to sneeze at.
Turning off fancy lighting can save 2-3 W easily.

Undervolting - 
Both the GPU and CPU should have considerable potential for undervolting with reduced clocks / power targets. The 1060 has some of the highest base and boost clocks in the Pascal family, so chances are it's pushed a fair way into diminishing returns territory by default. More power is cheaper than more silicon. With the Ryzen you have a good chance of actually improving performance if you give it a negative voltage offset at default power target.

OS - level (assuming Windows) -
Go through Task Manager looking for any applications sucking power for no good reason. RGB lighting software is a bit notorious here.
Update GPU drivers, it may help with power consumption. (_Team Red_ is generally reputed to be better-behaved in terms of ASPM, so long-term you might consider a 6600XT or something.)
Cap excessive frame rates to avoid needlessly driving up GPU power consumption.
If you have any SATA drives, make sure HIPM + DIPM are active (you need to change a registry setting to make AHCI link power management options appear in the power plan's settings). Note: Some older SATA SSDs don't play nice with DIPM and may require a firmware update.

text:
These cards are more efficient. The problem is not efficiency, but overall demand for output. Energy draw will never be a concern unless it is consciously made the top concern - and that takes political will and effort.
The necessity for ever-growing economic growth twists the general rule that Innovation is deflationary - be it in monetary terms, be it in consumption terms. Any gains in efficiency will be followed by a similar - AT LEAST - jump in consumption. The general trend is always to allow for a higher "Global Society TDP". The TDP will always be higher, and unfortunately for nerds like us that worship cool tech.... Tech innovation will NEVER be the answer, specially considering Climate Change.

There are other solutions that do not require you to fall in love with communist ideas, of course - like a GDP growth Cap with 0% as target. But the current standard will always follow this up. I don't wanna be the sucker in the room that states the obvious but.... Current capitalism is a design doomed to failure

author: @CanIHasThisName

text: @CanIHasThisName    I am not scared of the power consumption of this card, but on the precedent it makes. And to be clear this is not SLI. In SLI a single card did not increase the TDP, so the power draw increase did not have ripples on the industry and other lower end cards or form factors. If you design an architecture for high power, it might not be efficient on lower power draws to begin with, similar to how architectures designed for low power do not scale well when increasing the power (on this card 5% more performance on average for 30% more power). So I am scared for the 5060 and the RX 8600XT cards, and what will come of them. The 4000 and RX7000 is already there so it won't change much, however I heard that the 4000 series will increase the TDP even further. Imho, expect the future lower end SKUs to go up in power as well or probably be worse at performance  per watt, due to the design of higher end SKUs that come first and then need to be cut down. So it is not about this card, but what it will do to the GPU industry in two generations if they start designing them for this TDP. SLI was a better solution to the problem of the "I don't care about power" segment, and now with PCI-E 4 they have the bandwidth to do it perhaps even without SLI bridges and make it better. And SLi (when it was working) had much better scaling than this in terms of power, sometimes close to 1:1. The bad thing about it was the licensing and support because of it. But it is easier to just bump the power draw by a third for the 5% bragging rights. Point is: when somebody cares only about money it will do anything to get it, without caring about what are the repercussions, and this is what nVidia is doing, and we need to stop and teach them with by keeping out wallets shut.
author: @marsovac
@CanIHasThisName

text: @CanIHasThisName  The 3090/ti is GA102, which the same as the 3080 and is completely different to laptop chips which are GA104. My concern is not about laptops they have a limited power draw and the chips designed for them will have that in mind. I am concerned about the desktop segment, which uses mostly cut down dies to form new SKUs and not new designs like laptops. And of course SLI is dead, it was problematic to implement(support per game) and was never standardized, so it went extinct when process technology advanced. Was not saying that SLI is the solution but a better newer version of it that has less drawbacks and more compatibility or ease of implementation (possibly no implementation at all, just driver magic). The scaling it offered tough was much better than what we get with the "Ti" in the 3090 (5% performance for 100W). And the abysmal low end GPU generational scaling that you have seen compared to the high end might already be because of design choices favoring power. To reach high frequencies you need exponentially more power to get linear performance (if no bottlenecks). To reach high frequencies you need longer pipelines, which become less efficient on lower clocks and buses that are not as wide. And if you want to keep costs down you cut and reuse the same architecture whenever possible, making the 1050ti mobile faster than the desktop 1050ti, while the opposite happens on the high end and the high end laptop part has the performance of the previous generation desktop part. It will get worse than that, the low end desktop parts will become utter garbage if they want to keep the same lowend power draw and it will be better to game on a low end gaming laptop instead. This is my biggest concern that increasing power will have on the future. I don't want GPU development to favor the rich more than the poor (stagnation on the lower end to rake more on the high end and spend less in low end designs).

text:
The power draw requirements of modern gaming PCs with GPUs like this are getting ridiculous. I had to buy a separate dedicated UPS for mine (12900k, 3080Ti) as it was tripping out with other relatively low powered devices connected. High end "consumer" UPS devices (1500VA) only allow for a max wattage of 865w, meaning that even with a single high end PC, you get close to tripping the UPS. 

Also starting to raise concerns in general with gaming PC power consumption and the ability of home (or small office) electrical systems to run them. Most homes in the US have 15 amp circuits, which are often shared by a couple of rooms, meaning that with a max recommended continual load of 1440w (1880w max at 80%), you can run two high end gaming PCs but run very close to tripping a breaker, even without all the other devices that will be plugged in to the same circuit. Crazy.

text:
Governments aren't the solution. Customers will be... when they get their heads out of their asses, learn some self-control, educate themselves about computing (beyond superficial GPU benchmark stats) and start pressuring those companies to get the big guns out... but I can only dream.
Moore's law has been dead for long but even in the 60's IBM's researchers had already figured out a way out... among what is now a full repertoire of actual solutions for this problem (one of those solutions acting as a necessary foundation for the rest). Chipmakers are just falling prey to a sunken cost fallacy and they're aware that the end consumer doesn't actually know what's ultimately possible anyway... so the incentives to dust off their drawing boards isn't there.
Most end consumers (that's us) act as if those measly improvements between GPU generations are to be expected because they don't know where the ceiling is supposed to be. As a result, the status quo is maintained, innovation almost non-existent and inflation is about to swallow that industry whole. Hopefully it dies quickly and companies like Lightmatter get to lead a renaissance movement when it comes to computing efficiency.

I understand your point, but I'd like to make another one for the general societal trend. For that I'll be bending yours a little, although surely not in a unreasonable way.

They are more efficient. The problem is not efficiency, but overall demand for output. Energy draw will never be a concern unless it is consciously made the top concern - and that takes political will and effort.
The necessity for ever-growing economic growth twists the general rule that Innovation is deflationary - be it in monetary terms, be it in consumption terms. Any gains in efficiency will be followed by a similar - AT LEAST - jump in consumption. The general trend is always to allow for a higher "Global Society TDP". The TDP will always be higher, and unfortunately for nerds like us that worship cool tech.... Tech innovation will NEVER be the answer, specially considering Climate Change.

There are other solutions that do not require you to fall in love with communist ideas, of course - like a GDP growth Cap with 0% as target. But the current standard will always follow this up. I don't wanna be the sucker in the room that states the obvious but.... Current capitalism is a design doomed to failure.

text:
@houzeroze  Given the price difference it's still better to get a 3080 and play games well at 4k for the next 3-5 years, while saving the money for a future upgrade that will inevitably be far better than the 3090 at that point anyways. Going with the absolute top model is never a wise choice for longevity. It's only if you want absolute peak performance here and now and don't want any compromises regarding what is currently available. Sensible future proofing is buying the 2nd-in-line below the halo card, running it for as long as it can hold on, then getting a new gen of similar position once the performance jump makes the cost worth it.

Done this for years and my wallet is thanking me, and never have I had issues running modern titles on high settings at my given resolution (former 1080, then 1440 ultrawide)

text:
Nah.  Shareholders don't run the company. They only dictate the value of the company based on willingness to pay a certain price for a share or sell for a certain price.  If enough high volume shareholders got together, they could influence the voting of directors, but that is all.  The actual running of the company is independent of the shareholders.

I suspect the marketing group looked at the consumer data and realized that consumers were willing to purchase GPUs at a higher price than past history had suggested based on recent activity.  This was evident based on scalper prices.  By selling at higher prices, they were eliminating the scalpers and selling directly to consumers through their normal channels.  It probably results in more GPUs actually getting to consumers at MSRP instead of inflated scalper prices, even if the MSRP is higher than before.  The bonus for Nvidia is that they are the ones profiting, not some unintended middleman.  I'm not saying its right to take advantage of a situation like this, but capitalism will find a price point that works.  They will either sell all their GPUs at the inflated price, or the price will drop due to lack of demand at that price.  Either way, capitalism will determine the direction.

text:
@youtubeshadowbannedme  What are you on about? Tensor cores have nothing to do with Ray Tracing. Ray tracing is handled by Ray Tracing cores, not the Tensor cores. Both are extremely specialised at different tasks. 

The underlying technology of Tensor cores certainly isn't "exclusive" to Nvidia - although the specific implementation may be. 

"Tensor" comes from the term used to describe neural processing for deep learning. Tensor Core is just Nvidia's term for its implementation of specialised AI accelerator cores that can only make matrix calculations but are extremely efficient at it.

AMD already has their own equivalent counterpart to Tensor Cores but hasn't yet  used (or may not ever use) the tech in their consumer cards.

On the professional side, pretty much everyone involved with AI makes their own dedicated AI accelerator ASICs -  this not only includes hardware manufacturers like AMD, Nvidia, Samsung and Qualcomm but also those on the software side of AI such as Google, Apple and Amazon.

text:
I'm pretty ambivalent towards the increased power draw. I've seen a lot of people really slamming Nvidia for this and the rumoured 40 series specs, but if we want more and more performance, eventually power consumption is going to have to go up. You can't rely on lithography shrinks to keep it down forever.

Rising electricity prices and all that are good reasons to not actually own one of these, but from Nvidia's perspective it's a choice between releasing a product that performs identically to the previous one, or increasing the power draw (not that we see much perf gain here in this case, likely because near 400W 3090's are already pushing the silicon to its limit, but I think my point stands).
